lessons.title: A component returns a small UI tree
lessons.summary: Define Welcome to return an h1 reading Trail station, and have App use Welcome.
explanation: A React component is a function that describes part of the screen. React calls it while rendering. Start with one heading, not a whole application. In this course the runner renders App for you; you do not write an import or a mounting command.
Define Welcome to return an h1 reading Trail station, and have App use Welcome. The starter is the small application to edit; the examples above remain available for comparison.
steps: Read the small example and explain its inputs and effects.
Complete the starter for this lesson.
Run the behavior checks, then predict a changed case.

checks.label: Welcome also renders on its own
checks.expression: (() => { const host=document.createElement("div"); document.body.append(host); const root=ReactDOM.createRoot(host); try { ReactDOM.flushSync(()=>root.render(React.createElement(Welcome))); return host.querySelector("h1")?.textContent === "Trail station"; } finally { root.unmount(); host.remove(); } })()

quiz.question:
Welcome now returns

Route notes

, while App still returns . What appears?
choices: The word Welcome is printed as ordinary text
The original h1 stays because App did not change
quiz.explanation: React calls the component used by App and renders its returned description; App does not copy the old heading text.

hints: Trace the visible input, event and resulting screen before changing the code.

lessons.title: JSX inserts expression results
lessons.summary: Return a p with className="status" that shows Route: 8 by inserting the label constant and calculating stops + 2.
explanation: JSX can mix fixed markup with values calculated by JavaScript. Curly braces mark an expression whose result belongs in that position; text outside the braces stays literal. This lets the same markup describe changing data.

quiz.question:
With const level = 5, how does

level + 1: {level + 1}

read?
quiz.explanation: The first part is literal JSX text. Only the expression inside braces is evaluated.

lessons.title: Props configure separate component uses
lessons.summary: Define Pass to display its name prop. Render passes for Cedar and Fern in App; the same component must also display another supplied name.
explanation: Props are inputs passed to a component. Two uses of the same component can receive different values. Treat props as read-only: the component describes a result from its inputs rather than changing those inputs.

checks.label: Another name works
checks.expression: (() => { const host=document.createElement("div"); document.body.append(host); const root=ReactDOM.createRoot(host); try { ReactDOM.flushSync(()=>root.render(React.createElement(Pass,{name:"Meadow"}))); return host.textContent==="Meadow"; } finally { root.unmount(); host.remove(); } })()

quiz.question: App uses <Pass name="Oak" /> twice. How many paragraphs does this produce?
choices: One paragraph because the function has one definition
Two paragraphs that share and overwrite one name
quiz.explanation: Each JSX use asks React for its own component result, even when the prop values are equal.

lessons.title: Children compose a wrapper
lessons.summary: Define Panel to show its Notice h2 and its children. App should put a paragraph reading Bring a bottle. inside Panel.
explanation: A wrapper can provide a surrounding structure while its caller supplies the content inside. JSX nested between a component’s opening and closing tags becomes its children prop. The wrapper need not know every kind of content it will receive.

Define Panel to show its Notice h2 and its children. App should put a paragraph reading Bring a bottle. inside Panel. The starter is the small application to edit; the examples above remain available for comparison.

Complete the starter for this lesson.

checks.label: A different supplied child works
checks.expression: (() => { const host=document.createElement("div"); document.body.append(host); const root=ReactDOM.createRoot(host); try { ReactDOM.flushSync(()=>root.render(React.createElement(Panel,null,React.createElement("strong",null,"Closed today")))); return host.querySelector("strong")?.textContent === "Closed today" && host.querySelector("h2")?.textContent === "Notice"; } finally { root.unmount(); host.remove(); } })()

quiz.question: If App uses Closed today, must Panel be rewritten to support strong?
choices: No; props.children carries the supplied strong element
No; the strong element is discarded automatically
quiz.explanation: The wrapper inserts the received React content; it does not restrict that content to the earlier paragraph.

lessons.title: Pass a handler for React to call later
lessons.summary: Keep lastAction as none initially. Pass chooseMap as the Choose map button’s click handler so a click records map chosen, not during rendering.
explanation: An event prop receives a function to call when the event happens. Passing the function is different from calling it while rendering. Here the click records an action; it does not yet request a screen update. State is the next lesson.

Keep lastAction as none initially. Pass chooseMap as the Choose map button’s click handler so a click records map chosen, not during rendering. The starter is the small application to edit; the examples above remain available for comparison.

quiz.question: What is wrong with replacing onClick={chooseMap} by onClick={chooseMap()} here?
choices: It waits for two clicks instead of one
It records the action during render and passes the function’s return value
It passes exactly the same handler because parentheses are optional
quiz.explanation: Parentheses call a function now. The event prop needs the function value to call later.

lessons.title: State requests a new render
lessons.summary: Start the ticket count at 3 and add one for each separate click. Keep the button labeled Add ticket.
explanation: State is a value React remembers for a mounted component. A setter requests another render using the next state. Unlike changing the ordinary variable in the previous lesson, this updates the description React uses for the screen.
Start the ticket count at 3 and add one for each separate click. Keep the button labeled Add ticket. The starter is the small application to edit; the examples above remain available for comparison.

quiz.question: A fresh App starts at 3. After three separate clicks, what count is displayed?
choices: 4, because every click always uses the initial 3
quiz.explanation: Each separate event runs the handler from the latest committed render, so the count grows 3→4→5→6.

lessons.title: A handler reads one state snapshot
lessons.summary: Start at 2. Each Record click should increment count and report the count that the handler read before that increment.
explanation: A render gives its event handlers a snapshot of state. Calling a setter requests future state; it does not rewrite the local count variable in the handler that is already running. This matters when one event records the current value and also changes it.

quiz.explanation: The first event reads 2 and renders 3. The next event reads the new snapshot 3, then requests 4.

lessons.title: Queued updater functions compose
lessons.summary: Start at 1. Practice passing the pure increment updater twice per click, so one click displays 3 and another displays 5. The runnable checks assess those displayed results; the changed-example question distinguishes queued updaters from repeated replacement values.
explanation: When the next state depends on pending state, pass an updater function to the setter. React processes these queued updaters in order. Each receives the result of the previous update, rather than rereading one old handler snapshot.

quiz.question: A handler reads count 5 and calls setCount(count + 1) twice. What next count does it request?
quiz.explanation: Both replacement values are calculated from the same snapshot 5. Passing updater functions is what lets queued transformations build on one another.
